fixes.answer: [[On balance]], I think it is largely positive. Remote work offers people tremendous flexibility, eliminates stressful commutes and can improve work-life balance significantly. It also allows companies to hire talent regardless of location. However, it is not without drawbacks, such as isolation and blurred boundaries. So while I view it [[favourably]], its success depends on being managed thoughtfully rather than [[imposed]] without support.
fixes.why: 'thoughtfully' and 'support' are plain; marked 'on balance' and 'favourably'

fixes.answer: Absolutely, the suitability varies enormously. Knowledge-based, [[computer-centric]] jobs like writing, programming or design [[translate very well]] to remote work. However, roles requiring physical presence, such as healthcare, manufacturing or hospitality, simply cannot be done remotely. Even within office jobs, tasks needing intense collaboration or mentoring may suffer. So remote work is a wonderful option for some, but it is far from [[universally applicable]].
fixes.why: 'collaboration' is plain; merged 'universally applicable' into one phrase and marked 'computer-centric' and 'translate very well'

fixes.answer: The effects have been quite significant. As fewer people commute, some city centres have seen businesses that relied on office workers struggle. Conversely, remote work has allowed people to move away from expensive cities to smaller towns, potentially [[revitalising]] those areas. This [[redistribution]] of population could reshape [[urban planning]]. So it is causing a genuine, ongoing transformation of where and how people live.

It has a notable impact. On the positive side, it can reduce office politics and let people focus on their work. However, the spontaneous, informal interactions that build genuine [[camaraderie]] are much harder to replicate remotely. Relationships can become purely [[transactional]], and new employees in particular may struggle to feel connected. Maintaining a real sense of [[belonging]] requires deliberate effort in a distributed team.

I think hybrid working will become the [[dominant model]] rather than fully remote work. Most companies seem to be [[settling on]] a mix, valuing both the flexibility of home and the collaboration of the office. Fully remote roles will grow but remain a minority. So the future of work is likely to be flexible and varied, with people [[splitting their time]] according to what each task demands.
fixes.why: 'flexible', 'varied', 'demands' are plain; marked 'dominant model', 'settling on', 'splitting their time'

fixes.answer: Clear communication is absolutely key. Companies should set clear expectations while trusting employees rather than [[micromanaging]] them. Regular virtual check-ins and occasional in-person meetups help maintain connection and [[morale]]. Providing the right technology and supporting mental wellbeing are also crucial. Ultimately, engagement comes from a culture of trust and inclusion, ensuring remote staff never feel [[overlooked]] or forgotten.

The advantages are clear: no commute, greater flexibility, fewer office distractions and often improved work-life balance. Many people are genuinely more productive. The disadvantages include social isolation, difficulty separating work from home life, and potential distractions at home. [[Career progression]] can also suffer from being [[out of sight]]. So it offers real freedom, but demands strong [[self-discipline]] to manage well.

I largely disagree with that [[stereotype]]. While a lack of supervision might tempt a few, it seems that most remote workers are just as productive, if not more so, than their office counterparts. In fact, many overwork because the boundaries blur. Laziness is really a matter of individual discipline and motivation, not location. So I think this criticism is largely [[unfounded]] and rather [[outdated]].
fixes.why: 'discipline' is plain; marked 'stereotype'; softened 'the evidence suggests'
